strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important reliability problem at the intersection of multimodal NLP, chart question answering, and disinformation: MLLMs can be deceived by deliberately misleading visualizations.

The vulnerability study is broad, covering 18 open, proprietary, and chart-specialized models across multiple datasets and 17 misleader categories, while evaluating both QA accuracy and consistency on paired visualizations.

The main empirical finding is well supported: models often perform much worse on misleading charts, average misleading-chart accuracy is near the reported random baseline, and strong ChartQA performance does not reliably transfer to this setting.

The six inference-time corrections are clearly conceptualized and directly compared. Table-based QA gives large gains, while redrawing offers smaller improvements without significant losses on non-misleading charts in the reported experiments.
The paper is generally clear, with helpful examples, an appendix defining misleaders, statistical testing, and a stated commitment to release code and data.
weaknesses: The abstract claim that the effective methods improve misleading-chart QA 'without compromising accuracy on non-misleading ones' is too strong: the paper itself reports that table-based QA significantly reduces non-misleading accuracy for two models by up to 8.5 percentage points.

The correction evaluation is narrow. Only three 7B–9B open-weight models, all initially below the random baseline, are tested. The effectiveness of these methods on stronger models such as GPT-4o, Gemini, or the larger InternVL model remains unknown.

Table-based QA and redrawing depend on a separate text-only Qwen2.5-7B backend and on error-prone table extraction. The reported results therefore characterize a pipeline rather than a purely model-agnostic correction, and extraction/code-generation failures are not sufficiently ablated.

The aggregate misleading-versus-non-misleading comparison is not fully matched: the two sets have different sizes and composition, including real-world and VLAT examples on only one side. Item difficulty and dataset distribution may confound the reported 23.4-point average decline.

The random-baseline claim needs clarification because the misleading dataset includes MCQ, free-text, and ranking questions, but a 25% random baseline is directly meaningful only for four-way MCQ items. Scoring and baseline construction for the other formats should be specified.

Several categories have very few instances, including three categories with only one example, so per-category accuracies and claims about which misleaders are hardest are unstable. The Likert consistency study is also small, using only four visualization pairs covering three misleader types.

The methods assume substantial oracle information, especially the misleader-specific warning and known chart type. Since misleader detection itself is unsolved, the reported warning results are an upper bound and may not translate to a fully automatic deployment setting.

Multiple statistical tests are conducted across models, methods, and visualization pairs without discussion of multiplicity correction. Exact prompts, parsing rules, extraction outputs, API versions, and scoring criteria for free-text/rank answers should also be included to make the study fully reproducible.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and societally important problem: MLLMs can be misled by distorted visualizations and may thereby amplify disinformation.
It evaluates a broad suite of 18 MLLMs across vendors, model sizes, general-purpose and chart-specialized systems, providing a more comprehensive picture than studies limited to a single model.
The study combines accuracy evaluation, consistency evaluation on paired visualizations, and inference-time mitigation, giving several complementary views of the vulnerability.
The comparison against reported human performance on CALVI and CHARTOM and the use of paired significance tests strengthen the empirical analysis.
Table-based QA and redrawing show promising gains, and the paper honestly reports important failure cases such as table-extraction errors and limited redrawing success for complex charts.
The promised release of code and the newly annotated real-world multiple-choice examples would support future work on robust chart understanding.
weaknesses: The headline claim that performance falls to the random-baseline level is not fully verifiable: the misleading set combines MCQ, free-text, and ranking questions, but the paper does not explain how the single 25.6% random baseline was computed across these formats. Comparisons to ChartQA are also cross-task and cross-metric rather than strictly matched.

The abstract says performance can be improved without compromising non-misleading accuracy, but Experiment 3 reports that table-based QA causes significant decreases of up to 8.5 percentage points on non-misleading visualizations for two models. This is a material overstatement; only redrawing appears to avoid significant losses.

Correction results are narrow in scope. Only three open, mid-sized MLLMs are tested, so it is unclear whether the findings generalize to the 18 evaluated models or to commercial systems such as GPT-4o and Gemini.

Several methods assume oracle-like information: misleader warnings require knowing the defect in advance, axes/table extraction can fail, and redrawing assumes the chart type is known. Because no misleader detector is provided, the practical protective value and the title are somewhat oversold.

Table-based QA and redrawing use a fixed Qwen2.5-7B text-only model after extraction by the original MLLM. Improvements may therefore partly reflect substitution by a stronger text model rather than robustification of the original MLLM. Gold-table and same-model ablations are needed to isolate this effect.

Table extraction is not evaluated directly against ground-truth tables. The paper instead compares outputs from misleading and non-misleading versions, which cannot establish how accurate extraction itself is.

Experiment 2 uses only four visualization pairs and three misleader categories. Paired t-tests on eight ordinal Likert responses, with no apparent correction for multiple comparisons, provide weak support for broad claims about consistency.

Per-misleader conclusions are unstable because several categories have only one instance. Percentages such as 0% or 100% for these rare categories should not be treated as reliable evidence, even though the imbalance is acknowledged as a limitation.

Some aggregate misleading versus non-misleading comparisons are not fully matched—for example, CALVI contains 45 misleading but only 15 non-misleading instances, and the real-world subset has only misleading visualizations—so content and question difficulty may confound the reported gaps.

Given several concurrent 2025 studies already reporting MLLM vulnerability to misleading charts, the novelty rests primarily on the broader evaluation and simple correction pipelines; the claimed 'first' contributions need more careful differentiation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem at the intersection of multimodal NLP, chart understanding, visualization literacy, and model reliability. The threat setting is well motivated by real-world disinformation examples.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: 18 open, commercial, and chart-specialized MLLMs are evaluated across 17 misleader types, multiple datasets, MCQ/free-text/rank questions, and both accuracy and response-consistency settings.

The paired misleading/non-misleading visualization design strengthens the central vulnerability claim by holding the underlying data constant, and the Likert-scale consistency experiment complements the standard QA evaluation.
The paper contributes a new set of 42 real-world misleading visualizations with manually authored questions, increasing ecological validity beyond synthetic chart benchmarks.

The mitigation study is practically useful. Among six inference-time methods, table-based QA and redrawing the visualization show statistically significant gains, and the paper also examines the important trade-off with non-misleading chart performance.
The paper is clearly written and well illustrated, with helpful definitions of misleaders, model/implementation details, statistical tests, and a stated release of code and data.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction state that corrections improve misleading-chart QA without compromising non-misleading accuracy, but the results show that table-based QA causes significant decreases of up to 8.5 percentage points for two models. This claim should be qualified or restricted to the redrawing method.

Correction methods are evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight models that perform near or below random on the misleading set. The effectiveness and trade-offs of these methods for larger proprietary or chart-specialized models remain uncertain.

Several methods rely on privileged or error-prone information: misleader warnings require knowing the flaw, axes/table extraction depends on the same vulnerable multimodal models, and redrawing assumes known chart type and successful code generation. A fully automatic detection-and-correction pipeline is not demonstrated.

The misleading dataset is relatively small and highly imbalanced. Several misleader categories contain only one instance, so per-category rankings and claims about rare flaws such as overplotting or missing data should be treated as descriptive rather than robust findings.

Some evaluation details are under-specified, especially how free-text and rank answers are scored and how the random baseline is computed across heterogeneous question types. Exact numerical results and confidence intervals in addition to the bar charts would improve rigor and reproducibility.

The higher accuracy on real-world examples may be confounded by parametric knowledge, as the authors partly acknowledge. The experiment does not directly control for temporal overlap between model pretraining and the depicted events.
The manually created real-world questions would benefit from evidence of annotation validation, such as inter-annotator agreement or an ambiguity audit.

Several concurrent 2025 studies also examine MLLM vulnerability to misleading charts. The claimed novelty should therefore be scoped carefully around the particular breadth, consistency analysis, real-world data, and systematic correction-method comparison rather than only on being first.

Extraction and redrawing are evaluated mainly through downstream QA. The low exact table-match rate and possible semantic failures in successfully generated redrawings suggest that intermediate output quality needs more direct analysis.

strengths: Addresses a timely and high-impact problem at the intersection of multimodal NLP, chart question answering, and misinformation.
Provides broad empirical coverage: 19 MLLMs, 17 misleader categories, synthetic and real-world visualizations, and a newly introduced set of 42 real-world misleading charts with MCQs.
Combines complementary evaluations: ordinary QA accuracy, paired Likert-scale consistency, comparison with human performance, and systematic comparison of six inference-time interventions.

Reports actionable mitigation findings, especially that table-based QA and redrawing visualizations can remove or bypass misleading visual encodings, yielding gains of 15.4–19.6 percentage points on the tested models.

Supports reproducibility through zero-shot settings, temperature 0, detailed prompts in the appendices, statistical tests, code/data release, and extensive error analysis of table extraction and Chain-of-Thought variants.
weaknesses: The evaluation data are small and highly imbalanced: several misleader categories have only one instance, so per-type results such as 0.0% or 5.6% accuracy are unstable and should not be treated as robust category-level findings.

The aggregate misleading-versus-non-misleading comparison combines heterogeneous datasets, chart types, and question formats, often without paired visualizations. Causal claims about the effect of misleaders should therefore rely primarily on the paired CHARTOM and Likert experiments rather than the overall averages.

Mitigation methods are evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight models that performed below the random baseline in Experiment 1. Effectiveness on commercial, frontier, or chart-specialized models remains untested, limiting the generality of the protection claims.

The table-based QA condition uses a fixed text-only Qwen2.5-7B backend, so its comparison with methods that use the original MLLM confounds the correction strategy with the model performing the final QA.

Redrawing success is measured mainly by whether the generated Python code compiles. A compiled chart can still be semantically unfaithful because of upstream table-extraction errors; an end-to-end measure of redraw faithfulness is missing.

The abstract's statement that performance is improved 'without compromising' non-misleading accuracy is overstated: table-based QA degrades non-misleading performance by up to 8.5 percentage points, while only redrawing shows no significant decrease. The random-baseline calculation across MCQ, free-text, and ranking questions also needs clearer definition.

Higher accuracy on real-world charts may partly reflect parametric knowledge rather than robust visual interpretation. Although the authors discuss this confound, it still qualifies the real-world robustness conclusion.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important multimodal-NLP problem: robustness to deliberately misleading chart visualizations. It evaluates a broad range of 19 open, proprietary, and chart-specialized MLLMs across 17 misleader categories.

The vulnerability evidence is substantial: performance drops sharply on misleading visualizations, average accuracy approaches the random baseline, and high ChartQA performance does not transfer to robustness. The comparison with reported human accuracy further contextualizes the results.

The study goes beyond benchmarking by systematically comparing six inference-time correction methods and measuring both gains on misleading charts and degradation on non-misleading ones. Table-based QA and redrawn visualizations are identified as the most promising approaches, with McNemar tests used for the correction results.
The paper includes useful error analyses of the table- and axes-extraction stages, recognizes the error-propagation problem, and discusses parametric knowledge as a confound in the real-world subset.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: model families, temperature, dataset statistics, prompts, extraction procedures, and redrawing prompts are documented, and the authors state that code and several datasets will be released.
weaknesses: The mitigation results have limited generalizability because Experiment 3 uses only three mid-sized open-weight models, all of which performed below the random baseline in Experiment 1. The methods are not evaluated on stronger proprietary models or chart-specialized systems, so broad claims about protecting MLLMs remain under-supported.

The datasets are small and highly imbalanced. Several misleader categories occur only once, while the consistency experiment uses only four visualization pairs. Per-category accuracy rankings and statistical conclusions for rare categories are therefore unstable, and no multiple-comparison correction is reported.

Some aggregate misleading-versus-non-misleading comparisons combine datasets with different sources, question types, and difficulty levels. The paired comparisons within CHARTOM are more convincing and should be foregrounded to rule out dataset-selection effects.

The scoring protocol is under-specified for free-text and ranking questions, and the meaning of the reported random baseline across heterogeneous question formats is not fully explained. The real-world MCQs also lack reported annotation validation or inter-annotator agreement.

Real-world performance is confounded by parametric knowledge: models may answer from pretraining rather than from the visualization. The text-only controls are limited to a subset and mainly one model, so the magnitude of the visual vulnerability in this subset remains uncertain.

The proposed pipelines rely on prior knowledge of chart type and on error-prone extraction by the same MLLM. The main paper does not include oracle-table or oracle-axes ablations that would isolate mitigation effectiveness from extraction failure.

The practical protection remains modest: even the best corrections leave accuracy far below human performance, and table-based QA can reduce accuracy on non-misleading charts. The warning method also assumes ground-truth knowledge of the misleader, making it an upper-bound intervention rather than a directly deployable solution.

strengths: Addresses a timely and high-impact problem at the intersection of multimodal NLP, chart understanding, and visualization-driven misinformation.

Provides a broad empirical evaluation of 19 closed, open-weight, and chart-specialized MLLMs across synthetic, benchmark, and newly collected real-world visualizations, covering 17 types of misleaders.
Goes beyond vulnerability discovery by evaluating six inference-time mitigation methods and explicitly measuring the trade-off between gains on misleading charts and losses on non-misleading charts.

The central finding is compelling: average accuracy on misleading visualizations falls to 26.4%, close to the 25.6% random baseline, despite much stronger performance on ChartQA and non-misleading charts.

Combines accuracy evaluation with a Likert-scale consistency experiment, human-performance comparisons, per-misleader analysis, statistical testing, and detailed manual error analysis of table and axes extraction.

Table-based QA and visualization redrawing are identified as effective approaches, with gains up to 19.6 percentage points, and the paper carefully explains why removing or repairing the misleading visual channel helps.

Includes substantial reproducibility support through named model versions, zero-shot settings, temperature, prompts, statistical tests, and appendices describing extraction and redrawing pipelines; code and data release is promised.
The paper is clearly written and well illustrated, and its real-world dataset strengthens ecological validity beyond existing synthetic misleading-visualization benchmarks.
weaknesses: The datasets are relatively small and highly imbalanced: several misleader categories have only one instance, while the consistency study uses only four visualization pairs. Per-category conclusions and some significance tests are therefore noisy.

Aggregate misleading versus non-misleading comparisons combine heterogeneous sources and question formats, including MCQs, free-text questions, and ranking questions. The main text would benefit from a fuller explanation of answer extraction, scoring, and chance-level computation for each format.

Mitigation methods are evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight MLLMs that performed poorly in Experiment 1. Their effectiveness on frontier commercial models or specialized chart models remains uncertain.

The misleader-warning method is oracle-like because it assumes the correct misleader category and definition are known, and several pipelines also assume known chart type. The paper acknowledges this, but the methods are not yet directly deployable without a reliable detector.

Redrawn visualizations are accepted when the generated code compiles, but compilation does not guarantee that the redraw faithfully represents the underlying data, especially when table extraction is already incorrect or when chart types are unsupported.

Real-world results may be affected by parametric knowledge. The supporting analysis focuses mainly on GPT-4o and a subset of 22 questions, so it does not fully rule out memorization or temporal-cutoff effects across all models.

The new real-world annotations would be stronger with details about annotators, adjudication, and inter-annotator agreement. Reproducibility is also partially constrained by restricted access to CHARTOM and the research-only real-world data.

Many statistical comparisons are reported at p ≤ 0.05 without multiplicity correction or confidence intervals, and commercial API results appear to be evaluated in a single run despite possible nondeterminism.

The abstract's claim that correction improves misleading-chart performance 'without compromising' non-misleading accuracy should be qualified: table-based QA causes statistically meaningful drops of up to 8.5 percentage points for two models, although redrawing does not.

Given several concurrent 2025 studies on MLLM susceptibility to misleading charts, the novelty should be framed primarily as the larger-scale comparison, real-world evaluation, and mitigation analysis rather than as the first discovery of the vulnerability itself.
